results.result: The Tritonia swim CPG consists of three neuronal types (DSI, C2, VSI) that form a network producing rhythmic swimming behavior. C2 and VSI project through PdN6, and disconnecting this commissure impairs swimming.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C41 are well-supported by citations to established prior work (Getting, 1981, 1989b; Katz, 2007a, 2007b, 2009; Sakurai and Katz, 2009b) and anatomical data shown in Figure 1. This provides the foundational context for the study.

results.result: Cutting PdN6 significantly decreased body flexions 2 hours post-surgery compared to sham controls, with no pre-surgery differences. The coefficient of variance increased threefold in lesioned animals, revealing hidden population variability in lesion susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Levene median test) with N=19 animals. The experimental design includes proper controls (sham surgery) and multiple pre-surgery baseline measurements showing no initial differences (C5), strengthening the conclusion that lesion reveals hidden variability.

results.result: PdN6 disconnection significantly decreased VSI bursts per swim episode in isolated brain preparations, with coefficient of variance increasing from 0.16 to 0.47.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4B,C) with N=34 preparations and appropriate statistics (one-way repeated measures ANOVA, Levene median test). This recapitulates the behavioral findings at the circuit level and is consistent with prior work (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

results.result: C2 stimulation induced VSI bursts in 47/53 preparations with PdN6 intact, mostly via antidromic spikes (39/47). However, the number of C2-evoked VSI spikes did not correlate with swim motor pattern burst number under normal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are supported by experimental data from 53 preparations and appropriate statistical analysis (linear regression, R²=0.05, p=0.10). The lack of correlation under normal conditions (C14) is critical for establishing that this synaptic variability is 'hidden' under intact conditions.

results.result: After PdN6 disconnection, C2-evoked VSI depolarization amplitude significantly correlated with VSI burst number (R²=0.53) and inversely correlated with the extent of motor impairment (R²=0.47). Larger depolarizations predicted less impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are supported by strong correlations with appropriate statistics (linear regression, p<0.001, N=50) shown in Figures 6C,D. This demonstrates that the hidden synaptic variability becomes functionally relevant after lesion, a key finding of the study.

results.result: C2-evoked synaptic responses in VSI contain both monosynaptic and polysynaptic components. C2 stimulation causes prolonged EPSPs that are minimized by Hi-Di saline, revealing a biphasic monosynaptic potential with depolarizing and hyperpolarizing phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 and C47 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7A. The use of Hi-Di saline to isolate monosynaptic components is a standard and appropriate technique. This dissection of synaptic components is essential for identifying the source of variability.

results.result: The C2-evoked hyperpolarization in VSI (measured in Hi-Di saline) was larger and more variable (CoV=0.66) than the depolarization (CoV=0.42). The hyperpolarization amplitude inversely correlated with motor impairment (R²=0.44, p<0.001), indicating animals with stronger inhibition were more vulnerable to lesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C48-C49 are supported by statistical analysis (Levene median test, linear regression) from 26-56 preparations. The identification of the inhibitory component as the key predictor of vulnerability is a central finding. The variance analysis appropriately identifies this as the variable component.

results.result: The proximal VSI excitation is mainly caused by recruited polysynaptic EPSPs, not direct C2 excitation. However, the inhibitory component of the direct C2-to-VSI synapse, not polysynaptic recruitment, predicts lesion susceptibility. The inhibitory component limits polysynaptic EPSP effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53, C69-C71 are supported by experimental data showing no correlation between depolarization in normal vs Hi-Di saline (R²=0.04, p=0.37, N=24) but significant inverse correlation with hyperpolarization (R²=0.43, p<0.001). This mechanistic insight explains how inhibition gates the polysynaptic excitation and determines vulnerability.

results.result: VSI spike propagation direction varied among individuals: 24.6% showed only antidromic, 7.2% only orthodromic, and 68.1% mixed propagation. Animals with only orthodromic spikes were significantly less impaired by PdN6 disconnection than those with only antidromic spikes. VSI showed more antidromic spiking later in motor patterns, and these terminal antidromic bursts were preferentially lost after lesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 are supported by data from 69 animals with appropriate statistics (one-way ANOVA, F(2,66)=4.64, p=0.015). The correlation between spike initiation site and lesion susceptibility provides a mechanistic link between synaptic properties and functional outcome. Figure 8—figure supplement 1 provides additional supporting evidence.

results.result: Adding artificial C2-to-VSI inhibition via dynamic clamp did not affect burst number with PdN6 intact (N=18), but converted all VSI spikes to antidromic in all 16 preparations. This demonstrates the inhibition acts as a 'hidden' circuit change with no effect under normal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31, C55, C72-C75 are supported by dynamic clamp experiments from 16-18 preparations with appropriate statistics (paired t-test, p=0.16). The lack of effect with PdN6 intact is critical for establishing the 'hidden phenotype' concept. The conversion to antidromic spiking provides mechanistic insight into how inhibition controls spike initiation site.

results.result: Subtracting C2-to-VSI inhibition via dynamic clamp significantly increased VSI bursts per episode in 6/9 preparations with PdN6 intact, extending the motor pattern by causing more orthodromic spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C32 and C76 are supported by dynamic clamp experiments from 9 preparations (Figure 9). The increase in bursts when inhibition is removed provides complementary evidence that inhibition normally limits motor pattern duration, though this effect is modest under intact conditions.

results.result: After PdN6 blockade, adding artificial C2-to-VSI inhibition via dynamic clamp further decreased VSI bursts from 25% to approximately 60% reduction compared to control, making preparations more susceptible to lesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C78-C79 are supported by dynamic clamp experiments from 20 preparations with appropriate statistics (paired t-test, p<0.0001). This demonstrates that artificially increasing inhibition increases vulnerability, providing causal evidence for the role of this synapse in determining lesion susceptibility.

results.result: Subtracting C2-to-VSI inhibition via dynamic clamp after PdN6 disconnection restored VSI bursts from 27.7% below control to 3.3% above control (p=0.003, N=19), partially rescuing vulnerable preparations. The effect was more pronounced in vulnerable preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C57, C80-C81 are supported by dynamic clamp experiments from 19 preparations with significant statistics (paired t-test, p=0.003). This rescue experiment provides strong causal evidence that the inhibitory synapse determines vulnerability. The greater effect in vulnerable preparations (C80) is consistent with the correlation data.

results.result: Artificial reduction of inhibitory conductance enhances C2-evoked depolarization through recruited EPSPs, making the proximal VSI spike initiation zone more excitable.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is a mechanistic inference that logically follows from the experimental data showing that subtracting inhibition increases bursts and causes orthodromic spiking. This explanation is consistent with the established role of inhibition in gating polysynaptic excitation (C69-C71).

results.result: VSI has two spike initiation zones (one per pedal ganglion) capable of independent firing with different propagation directions. Multiple spike initiation zones provide circuit resilience by offering a backup after lesion. Susceptibility depends on the primary spike initiation zone location.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by prior work (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b) and current data (Figure 8). The inference that multiple spike initiation zones provide resilience (C61) is well-supported by the correlation between spike direction and lesion susceptibility (C27). This provides a mechanistic framework for understanding individual differences.

results.result: The strength of the inhibitory C2-to-VSI synapse does not affect intact circuit function but determines lesion susceptibility, serving as a hidden phenotype that predicts circuit disruption vulnerability.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C56 synthesize the major findings: no correlation under normal conditions (C14), strong correlation after lesion (C15-C17, C22), and dynamic clamp causality (C30, C33, C37). This 'hidden phenotype' concept is the central conclusion and is well-supported by converging evidence.

results.result: Subtle synaptic differences between animals had no behavioral relevance under normal conditions but caused differential vulnerability to brain lesion. Motor impairment correlated with VSI spike initiation site, determined by inhibitory synapse strength. Artificially manipulating this synapse altered lesion susceptibility without affecting normal function. Neural circuit differences could serve as hidden phenotypes for predicting outcomes of neural damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 represent the main conclusions of the study. They are well-supported by the behavioral data (C4-C8), circuit recordings (C9-C10, C15-C17, C22-C23, C27), and causal dynamic clamp experiments (C30, C33, C37). The 'hidden phenotype' concept (C46) is appropriately framed as a suggestion rather than a definitive conclusion.

results.result: C2 burst number was largely unaffected by dynamic clamp, likely because manipulation was applied to only one VSI of the bilateral pair and C2 is electrically coupled to its contralateral counterpart.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is a reasonable inference explaining why C2 was not affected by the manipulation. The explanation is consistent with known bilateral organization and electrical coupling in the circuit. This is a minor technical point that does not affect the main conclusions.

results.result: Prior work has established that individual animals can exhibit similar behaviors despite substantial neural variability, and that individual differences in humans impair outcome prediction after brain injury or stroke. Axonal injury in white matter plays complex roles in disrupting neural networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40, C65-C67 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims establish the broader context and significance of the study. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: This is the first direct analysis of synaptic variation affecting vulnerability of a neuronal circuit to a particular lesion.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is a novelty claim that cannot be fully verified without comprehensive knowledge of all prior literature. While the authors state this is to their knowledge the first such analysis, this type of claim is inherently uncertain and depends on the authors' literature review being complete.
